How Cortisol Affects Decisions Made by Founders
How long term stress changes the decisions founders make.
How Cortisol Affects Decisions Made by Founders

Founders sometimes make decisions while tired and under pressure, for example hiring a person quickly to fill a vacant role, turning down a partnership to avoid uncertainty, or sending an email that should have stayed as a draft. Research on cortisol and decision making gives a specific explanation. Founders under pressure for a long time are not only more stressed. Their brains process decisions differently in measurable ways.
What cortisol does to the part of the brain used for planning

Cortisol is the main stress hormone in the body. In short periods it is useful. It raises blood sugar, increases attention and helps form memories of important events. Problems begin when levels stay high, or rise too often, for weeks at a time.
The prefrontal cortex becomes less active

The prefrontal cortex sits behind your forehead. It handles weighing options, keeping a long term plan in mind, stopping an impulse and changing course when evidence changes. It is also one of the parts of the brain most affected by stress.

Work by Amy Arnsten at Yale describes how high levels of stress chemicals quickly weaken networks in the prefrontal cortex. Under short term stress the effect is temporary. Under long term stress, studies have found structural changes too, with connections in the prefrontal cortex becoming thinner while circuits in the amygdala become stronger.
The amygdala has more influence

As control by the prefrontal cortex weakens, other systems have more influence. The amygdala, which is central to fear and threat detection, and circuits linked to habits guide more behaviour. You use familiar patterns and react faster. That helps when escaping danger. It is less suited to choosing a pricing strategy.
Under long term stress, control shifts from the part of the brain that plans to the parts that detect threats and follow habits. Reactions become faster and judgement becomes poorer.
How cortisol affects decisions made by founders
The shift from deliberate to reactive thinking produces three patterns that will be familiar to anyone who has run a company through a hard year.
1. Focus on the short term

A stressed brain gives less weight to the future. When the prefrontal cortex is under strain, immediate relief carries more weight than long term value. In practice that can mean cutting the brand budget to improve one month of numbers, accepting a customer who is a poor fit because the revenue is certain, or delaying infrastructure work that would save the team months next year.
2. Avoiding risk at the wrong times

You might expect stress to make people reckless. Often it does the opposite, and at the wrong time. A study published in PNAS in 2014 by Kandasamy and colleagues raised participants' cortisol over eight days with hydrocortisone to mimic a prolonged stressful period. Their risk aversion increased by 44 percent.
When cortisol was kept elevated for eight days, participants became 44 percent more risk-averse in financial decisions.

The researchers had earlier observed the same pattern in real traders. Cortisol rose as markets became more volatile. Prolonged stress makes people most cautious when markets are most uncertain. For a founder, that can mean passing on a change in direction, a senior hire or a funding round.
3. Hiring and leaving decisions made quickly

Long term stress also lowers the point at which people act to end discomfort. A research review by Starcke and Brand found that stress pushes people towards quick, intuitive choices and away from careful analysis, especially when the decision feels threatening. Founders under pressure hire the first plausible candidate to remove a problem, dismiss a person too quickly to relieve tension, or consider selling the company at the lowest point of a cycle to stop the feeling.
None of these choices feels impulsive at the time. A stressed brain is very good at generating reasons for what it already wants to do.
Cortisol and negotiation results
Negotiation is decision making under social pressure, and it is where the effect of cortisol can cost money.

Studies of negotiation and stress hormones suggest that people with higher cortisol before a negotiation tend to take a more defensive position. They make fewer creative offers, give up points they care about earlier, or hold positions that do not serve them. Short term stress has also been shown to make people more sensitive to how a choice is presented, so a term presented as a loss can feel far more threatening than the same term presented as a gain.
Combine that with the effects of poor sleep, which we cover in

, and a founder arriving at a discussion of funding terms after weeks of pressure is negotiating at a disadvantage.
How to restore activity in the prefrontal cortex
You cannot remove pressure from building a company. You can reduce how much that pressure controls your decisions.
Separate the decision from the moment you first consider it.

For any choice with consequences lasting more than a quarter, such as hires, exits, pricing or funding terms, use a 24 hour rule. Write the decision and your reasoning, then review it after a night of sleep.
Lower your usual stress level, not only the highest points.
Regular moderate exercise, consistent sleep and a short daily breathing practice all help restore the cortisol rhythm. Our breakdown of
the founder stress response
sets out three interventions with research behind them.
Use another person to review the decision.

A trusted cofounder, adviser or board member who is not under the same pressure can provide the planning perspective you may be missing. Ask them one question. What would you do if you were not tired and worried?
Measure your condition before large decisions.
A quick daily rating of stress and sleep turns a general feeling of pressure into numbers you can act on.
Know when your judgement is affected

Cortisol does not feel like impaired judgement. It can feel like clarity and urgency. The reliable protection is to know your condition before you make the decision.
